clue.text: Conservative cuts make things easier to swallow

parts.note: to hew is to cut, as with an axe

explanation.surface: A Tory reduction in spending is offered as a way to make policies easier for voters to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts' reads as spending cuts but is the verb, HEWS; 'swallow' is literal eating, not accepting.
explanation.definitionFit: Grinding food with the teeth is what makes it easier to get down the throat.

clue.text: March I as arranged for personal gift

indicators.note: the letters are set out as arranged, in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone's March birthday present is arranged by the person themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as arranged' rearranges MARCH I; the leftover 'for' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic personal appeal is an innate talent, a gift of personality.

clue.text: Capital area in which to reconstruct sand-tee

indicators.note: to reconstruct something is to rebuild it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A golf course in the city needs its sandy tee rebuilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reconstruct' rearranges SAND-TEE. The East End is the area of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: London's eastern districts, round Whitechapel, are a part of the capital city.

parts.note: to peer is to look closely, to pry

explanation.surface: A lord of high society is agile on his feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' looks like a noble; it is the verb, to look closely.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively and active, especially of an older person, is being agile.

clue.text: Don't count workers in winter sports gear

parts.note: to skip something is to pass over it without counting it
worker ants are the crossword's standard workers

explanation.surface: A list of workers in skiing clothes is passed over in a headcount.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers worn on the slopes are clothing for skiing, a winter sport.

parts.note: a chess piece that moves in an L, combined with an unmarried man unlikely to find a partner

explanation.walkthrough: 'mate' looks like checkmate; it means to marry. A knight bachelor is a knight of no order, the lowest rank of knighthood.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain knighthood outside any order is so titled, and literally reads as an unmarried knight.

parts.note: to pip is to blackball or fail a candidate in an exam

explanation.surface: A student fails the exam in English and weeps.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'pipe one's eye' is old slang for crying, so the verb alone can mean to weep.
explanation.definitionFit: Shedding tears was once called piping one's eye, so the verb here means to cry.

clue.text: Ne plus ultra elements on the fence?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the elements of the word are broken apart and put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: The very best in a chemistry lab is undecided about which elements to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plus' joins NE to the rearrangement of ULTRA, which 'elements' signals. Ne plus ultra is Latin for the highest point.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitting on the fence means taking no side in a dispute.

parts.note: an edge is a small lead over a rival

explanation.surface: A gardener finds a plant gives the south side of the garden the advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: A grass-like marsh plant is a kind of vegetation.

parts.note: the royal yacht was named for the female figure of Britain, and the clue pretends a tin alloy is named after the ship

explanation.walkthrough: Britannia was the British royal yacht; the alloy is a pewter-like tin alloy with antimony and copper.
explanation.definitionFit: A silvery mix of tin, antimony and copper is a metal alloy used for tableware.

definitions.meaning: an insurer, one who takes on a risk for a premium

explanation.definitionFit: An insurance company issuing life cover is called this, and the word also literally names anyone who reassures.

parts.note: read as figures, 1 is the Roman I and 1,000 the Roman M
the £ sign stands for a pound

explanation.surface: A thousand pounds is the cost of getting a car back from a car park.
explanation.walkthrough: The sum is read symbol by symbol: 1 = I, 1,000 = M, £ = POUND. A car pound is where seized cars are held, so to impound is to hold one up there.
explanation.definitionFit: Towed vehicles are seized and kept in a compound, so the verb means to confiscate and detain.

parts.note: the ill-omened date in March of the Roman calendar on which Julius Caesar was killed, the end of a classical hero

explanation.walkthrough: 'march-time' suggests the rhythm of a military march; it is the month of March, whose middle day the soothsayer warned Caesar to beware.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifteenth of March in the Roman calendar is the day of Caesar's assassination, long held unlucky.

clue.text: Feeling first signs of impetigo, the cutis having yellowed?

indicators.note: the first signs of several words are their opening letters, taken one from each

explanation.surface: A patient notices the early symptoms of a skin infection, the skin having turned yellow.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a medical description, and impetigo does make skin itch, so the definition fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Having an urge to scratch is a sensation the skin feels.

parts.note: to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: Now is the proper moment to feel sorry.
explanation.definitionFit: Correct and accurate are both senses here, as in a straight and accurate line.

definitions.meaning: in common or slang use, to eat greedily
an object of derision, a laughing-stock

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for wolfing food down, and also an object of jeering contempt.

parts.note: OPS is short for opuses, works of music

explanation.surface: Roadworks in the street hold up the traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street works' looks like roadworks; it is ST and OPS, where op. is a composer's numbered work.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevent or halt is to hinder.

parts.note: a specific is a remedy for a particular disease, so a holder for a specific is one for a remedy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Specific' looks like an adjective; it is the old noun for a remedy aimed at one illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass vessel for a liquid remedy holds a specific, an old word for a targeted cure.

clue.text: Form of brief ambition to favour

indicators.note: a new form of the word means its letters are rearranged

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A short form of an ambitious plan is written to win support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of' rearranges BRIEF into BEFRI.
explanation.definitionFit: To act as a friend to someone is to show them support and kindness.

clue.text: Slips field-nice change in such auto-control

indicators.note: a change in the letters signals they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket captain rearranges the slips in the field to show restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' turns SLIPS and FIELD-NICE (fourteen letters) into the answer; slips are close catching positions behind the batsman in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Control of oneself, exercised by one's own will, is mastery over impulses.

clue.text: Put new life into England's openers, not recorded by name

indicators.note: the openers of the word are its opening letters, as opening batsmen start an innings

parts.note: a live broadcast is not recorded

explanation.surface: England's opening batsmen are revitalised in a match shown live and named.
explanation.walkthrough: 'openers' takes two letters here, EN, since openers come in pairs in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To animate or invigorate is to give fresh spirit.

clue.text: Upside down — like this due, made for you

definitions.meaning: inverted, turned the other way up

definitions.text: like this due, made for you
definitions.meaning: these words rhyme, so the clue is written ...

explanation.definitionFit: Inverted order is one sense; the rhyming line, due and you, is written in poetry, the other.

definitions.meaning: a shaft drilled into the ground from which oil is drawn
in good order, as in 'all is fine'

explanation.definitionFit: A drilled shaft yields oil, and the adverb also means fine or in good health.

parts.note: a bereaved wife may need help, and in some card games an extra hand dealt face down has the same name

explanation.walkthrough: 'hand' looks like help; in games such as five hundred the spare hand of cards is called the widow.
explanation.definitionFit: A wife whose husband has died, and the name of a spare hand of cards dealt in some games.

indicators.note: a fish wriggling twists about, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bronze-coloured freshwater fish wriggles on the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wriggling' rearranges BREAM. The grid as printed reads AMEER, but the anagram and definition both give AMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: Fossil resin has a brownish-yellow colour, and the colour takes its name.

indicators.note: half of a word is its first four of eight letters here

parts.note: means in arithmetic are averages

explanation.surface: Someone means to make an announcement, but only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means' is not 'intends' but the plural noun from statistics, AVERAGES; 'Half' keeps its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: To state firmly or assert is to declare.

indicators.note: the words show the letters within them, run together across the gap

explanation.surface: Froth appears on the lakes of Cumbria, England's Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer of froth or impurity on a liquid is surface foam.

parts.note: Kit is the short form of the name Christopher

explanation.surface: A traveller removes a Saint Christopher medal for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' looks like removing; it means to parody.
explanation.definitionFit: A short comic sketch mimicking someone is a parody, a take-off.

clue.text: Home for innocent things receiving bills?

definitions.text: Home for innocent things receiving bills?

parts.words: Home for innocent things receiving bills?
parts.note: doves are emblems of innocence, and their bills are beaks, not accounts; a cot is a small shelter

explanation.walkthrough: 'bills' looks like invoices to a household; it is birds' beaks.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelter for pigeons and their kin houses birds that symbolise innocence.

clue.text: O.E. taker, in a way, of royal refugee

indicators.note: in a way of its own, the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A student of Old English is described as the one who took in a fleeing king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges O.E. and TAKER. After the Battle of Worcester in 1651 the future Charles II hid in an oak at Boscobel, the Royal Oak.
explanation.definitionFit: The fugitive Charles II hid in one at Boscobel, so the Royal Oak belongs to the royal refugee.

clue.text: This theatre will mind being renovated

indicators.note: a building being renovated is reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre's owner will not object to the building being refurbished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being renovated' rearranges WILL MIND. The Windmill was a London theatre in Soho, famous for staying open through the Blitz.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windmill Theatre in Soho is the London playhouse named.

clue.text: Harris is one in the river

definitions.meaning: Harris is a woollen cloth from the Outer Hebrides
a river forming part of the Scotland-England border

explanation.definitionFit: Harris cloth is a rough woollen fabric of this type, and the river is the one on the Scottish border.
